hero.title: Your Skills, Gaps & Support Network.
hero.intro: Recognise what you can already do, identify the one gap that matters next, and plan how to learn or ask for help. Your deliverable is a Skills & Support Map.

fields.label: What is your next useful venture task?
fields.placeholder: Understand how visitors follow up after an event.
fields.hint: Use an action from Lesson 02 or choose a small discovery task.

fields.label: Which strengths can you use for that task?
fields.placeholder: Organising conversations, listening, and keeping notes.
fields.hint: Name two or three relevant abilities; be specific about what you can do.

fields.label: What examples support those strengths?
fields.placeholder: I coordinated a small event team and kept an agreed schedule.
fields.hint: Say what you did and what happened. Keep sensitive names and details out.

fields.label: Which one skill or access gap matters most now?
fields.placeholder: I need to practise writing neutral questions before speaking with visitors.
fields.hint: Connect the gap to the task, rather than listing everything you lack.

fields.label: How will you learn, practise, use a tool, or get help?
fields.placeholder: Draft three questions and rehearse with a peer for 20 minutes Thursday.
fields.hint: Choose a route, action, time limit and an observable learning result.

fields.label: Who or which role could help, and what is their status?
fields.placeholder: A peer with research experience; request planned, not confirmed.
fields.hint: Use roles or aliases. State relevant experience and whether help is only planned, requested, or agreed.

fields.label: What specific support request will you make?
fields.placeholder: Could you review three discovery questions for 15 minutes this week and comment by Friday?
fields.hint: Include context, help, time, output and review point. Draft only; nothing is sent.

fields.label: What is your fallback and review point?
fields.placeholder: Use the lesson guide to revise the questions, practise alone, and review Friday.
fields.hint: If help is unavailable, what will you simplify or do next, and when will you review?

fields.label: What access or resource constraint should you flag?
fields.placeholder: Optional: availability, cost, time or access to a suitable learning source…

fields.label: Which claimed strength still needs a stronger example?
fields.placeholder: I say I can… but I need to check this by…

fields.label: How will you check whether the learning or support route helps?
fields.placeholder: I will look for… If that does not happen, I will…

fields.label: What could go wrong if the planned helper is unavailable or unsuitable?
fields.placeholder: The risk is… My fallback or pause point is…

questions.prompt: How should you choose the first skill gap to work on?
options: Choose the gap most relevant to the next useful task
List every possible skill and learn them all first
questions.explanation: Tie the priority gap to the next task; skills that are not needed yet can wait.

questions.prompt: What makes a claimed strength more useful?
options: A concrete example of what you did and what happened
A confident label without an example
questions.explanation: Examples help you assess capability for the specific work ahead.

questions.prompt: How should you describe a possible helper before they agree?
options: As potential support with the request status clearly stated
questions.explanation: Availability and commitment need agreement. A contact or draft request is not confirmed help.

blocks.prompt:
Create an engaging beginner-friendly explainer for LYNQ Venture Studio Academy, Module 1.1 Lesson 04: “Your Skills, Gaps & Support Network.” Desired final edit: approximately 150 seconds, 16:9, 1080p. Combine calm documentary workplace cutaways, simple animated diagrams and a real worksheet screen recording. Palette: navy #0B2338, teal #087D79, mint #BCF2DF, white. Contemporary Dubai setting, diverse adults, friendly plain-language English narrator. Use believable learning and collaboration moments, not dramatic success imagery.

Teaching goals: connect strengths to concrete examples; derive the priority skill gap from the next venture task; choose a proportionate learn/practise/tool/help route; make a specific respectful request; distinguish potential support from confirmed help; and plan a fallback. No skill/personality diagnosis, hiring guarantees, real contact names, invented endorsements, traction or claims that tools replace qualified expertise. Use a FICTIONAL event coordinator who can organise events but needs to practise neutral customer questions. Label the case “Illustrative example.”

Use the six scenes below in order. Target about 25 seconds per scene in the final edit, allowing natural narration timing and diagram holds. Record one consistent voice track separately. Generate short visual shots only in durations supported by the selected Gemini/Veo model; an eight-second shot plan is optional where supported. Assemble footage, diagrams, narration and screen recording in an editor. Do not claim a single generation will create the entire polished lesson.

Return a storyboard, edit timings and separate visual-generation prompts first. No generated visible text, logos, captions, watermark, speaking presenter or fabricated UI. Exact LYNQ wordmark, scene labels, arrows and diagrams must be editable post-production elements. Suggested diagrams: Next task → Required skill → Existing evidence → Priority gap; Learn / Practise / Tool / Ask for help; Possible contact → Request planned → Confirmed help; Task + Specific ask + Time + Output + Review point. Keep the same approved actor reference and wardrobe across continuity shots. Use realistic hands and respectful peer collaboration.

Scene 6 must use an actual screen recording of the approved Lesson 04 worksheet with fictional data, rather than generated product UI. Do not expose personal phone numbers, private contact lists or confidential client information. End card added in post: “Use your strengths. Close one gap. Make one clear ask.” A planned request must never appear as a confirmed commitment.

Final human-produced deliverables: H.264 1920×1080 MP4, editable project and diagrams, narrator audio, thumbnail, timed English VTT/SRT and transcript, generation/reference rights record. Produce separate native-reviewed Arabic narration/captions and RTL graphics; do not auto-mirror English UI. sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Build capability around the next useful step.

children: You do not need to be an expert in every part of a business. You need to understand the next task, recognise what you can contribute, and plan how to close the gaps that could stop you doing it well.
A
skill
is something you can do. A
gap
is a capability or access you still need for a particular task. A
support network
includes people you may learn from, get feedback from, or work with. Possible support becomes a commitment only when the person agrees.
By the end, you can
Name useful strengths with concrete examples.
Choose one skill gap based on the next venture task.
Compare learning, practice, tools and outside help.
Draft a specific support request without assuming agreement.
Set a fallback and review point.
Step 1 · Start with the task

Use your Lesson 02 Responsibility Map. If your next step is to understand visitors’ experiences, you may need listening, question planning and note-taking. A polished app, large team or extensive branding may come later.
Step 2 · Look for evidence of your strengths

“I coordinate event teams and kept a small project on schedule” tells you more than “I’m a natural leader.” Examples may come from paid work, school, community work, caregiving or personal projects. Say what you did and what happened. Keep experience at the level you can actually support.
Useful strengths
Listening, organising, explaining, designing, selling, research, problem-solving, practical delivery and knowledge of a community can all contribute.
No one needs to bring all of them.
A priority gap
The gap matters because it affects a specific next task. “I need to practise asking neutral questions” is more actionable than “I need to know everything about business.”
Choose one gap to work on first.
Step 3 · Choose a proportionate route
Learn
Use an approved lesson, guide or experienced person to understand the method. Choose a source and a small learning outcome.
Practise
Try the skill in a small situation and get feedback. Rehearse questions with a peer before using them with customers.
Use a tool
A calendar, worksheet or software tool can help with execution. Check outputs and permissions; a tool does not automatically supply sound judgment.
Ask for help
A peer, mentor, collaborator or specialist may help. Explain the task and check their relevant experience, availability and expectations.
Follow one illustrative example

An event coordinator can organise people but has little experience interviewing visitors. Their next task is to understand what happens after an event. They choose interview planning as the priority gap, draft three neutral questions, practise with a peer, and request a short review. The peer has not agreed yet, so the map labels that support as
request planned

blocks.prompt: You can coordinate an event, but you are unsure how to ask neutral discovery questions. Your next task is to understand visitors. What fits best?

options.label: Hire a full product team now
options.feedback: Match the gap to the next task. A full team may be premature, and experience in one area does not prove every skill. Start with focused practice and a clear request.

options.label: Practise questions and request feedback
options.feedback: Useful choice: practise the specific skill needed for the next task, then request feedback. Confirm the helper’s availability and keep a fallback.

options.label: Assume your experience covers every skill
options.feedback: Match the gap to the next task. A full team may be premature, and experience in one area does not prove every skill. Start with focused practice and a clear request.

children: Optional practice; the scored knowledge check is below.
Step 4 · Make a clear support request
A useful request says:
what I’m doing, the help I need, time involved, output, and review point.
Example: “I’m preparing three questions to understand event follow-up. Could you review whether they are neutral? I’m asking for 15 minutes this week, with comments on the question list by Friday.”

Ask before sharing private information, respect a no, and clarify any fee or ongoing commitment. For specialist work with important consequences, verify relevant qualifications and experience. Write roles or aliases in this prototype instead of private contact details.
A possible contact is not confirmed support.
Distinguish “person/role to approach,” “request planned,” “awaiting reply,” and “agreed help.” This worksheet records your plan and does not contact anyone.
Step 5 · Have a fallback

If help is unavailable, can you simplify the task, practise first, find another suitable source, or pause? Set a date to review what you learned. A support map is useful when it leads to a realistic action, not just a list of impressive names.
Connect the next task to strengths you can show, one priority gap, and one practical support action. You can begin with self-learning; outside help is not required to complete this lesson.
Arabic entries use automatic text direction. Use roles or aliases instead of private contact details. Lesson 04 saves separately.
This is a draft plan. No request is sent, and no person’s availability or agreement is verified. Local storage is plaintext; download a copy before changing browsers.
Simulated Coach · no AI connection
Try four scripted guidance modes. The preview reads your current worksheet locally; it does not send information anywhere.

replies.teach: A useful skill gap comes from the next task. Name strengths with examples, choose one missing capability, then decide whether to learn, practise, use a tool or ask for help. Potential support is not confirmed until someone agrees.
replies.guide: Start with one task from your Responsibility Map. Which abilities can you demonstrate? What one gap could stop the task? Choose a small learning action and draft a clear request with time, output and a fallback.
replies.review:
Skills & Support Map check: {missing} required fields still empty. All eight map entries are present. Check the evidence for strengths, the task-to-gap link, support status, request scope and fallback.
This scripted check only counts fields. It cannot assess competence, verify qualifications or confirm anyone’s agreement.
replies.challenge: Are you choosing a gap that matters now? What evidence supports your claimed strength? Is the person available and suitable? What will you do if they decline? Avoid treating a planned request as a commitment.
